Intramolecular [5 + 2] cycloaddition reactions of oxidopyrylium ylides
provide rapid access to privileged bridged seven-membered polycyclic
structures. In particular, type II variants provide convenient access to
highly strained adducts bearing an anti-Bredt double bond. However,
enantioselective variants using catalytic methods remain unknown. Here
we report an enantioselective method enabled by a non-covalent activation
strategy using chiral acid catalysis. The use of a suitable leaving group
in the oxidopyrylium precursor and an efective chiral-phosphoric-acid
catalyst are crucial to the process. Multiple stereogenic centres can be
constructed in one step with high eficiency and excellent enantioselectivity
and diastereoselectivity under mild conditions. The products generated
from this process are not only structurally intriguing but also represent
core structures or advanced intermediates found in natural products.
Both mechanistic experiments and computational calculations reveal that
enolization is the rate-determining step, whereas the cycloaddition is the
enantiodetermining step.

precursor, such as an acetal (Fig. 1c), a chiral acid catalyst might be
able not only to promote the first step but also catalyse the cycload-
dition step and provide the essential facial discrimination by form-
ing a hydrogen bond with the oxidopyrylium. It should be noted,
however, that such an asymmetric induction via weak activation
by a chiral catalyst is unprecedented even for the limited examples
of type I cycloadditions, where the formation of a covalent bond
between the amine catalyst and substrate is required for effective
enantiocontrol, as pioneered by Jacobsen, Reyes and Vicario<sup>26–28</sup>.

system, which represents the first catalytic enantioselective type II
[5 + 2] cycloaddition of oxidopyryliums, providing efficient access
to a range of functionalized, oxygen-bridged polycyclic molecules
with excellent enantioselectivities and diastereoselectivities under
mild conditions.
Results and discussion
Reaction development
First, a family of pyranones 1 with the olefinic dipolarophiles tethered
at the 3-positions was prepared for reaction as the oxidopyrylium
precursors. In our initial attempts, we used acetoxypyranone 1aa as
substrate because this is a common precursor to oxidopyrylium ylides,
although they are typically generated under basic conditions<sup>30–33</sup>.
Unfortunately, in the presence of a chiral-phosphoric-acid (CPA)
catalyst, no reaction was observed (Table 1, entry 1). We also tried
the dual catalytic system with a chiral amine and an achiral thiourea,
developed for the type I cycloaddition by Jacobsen and co-workers<sup>26</sup>;
however, this system proved ineffective for the type II cycloaddition
(see Supplementary Table 1 for details). To improve the reactiv-
ity, hydroxypyranone 1ab was examined with the expectation that
acid-catalysed dehydration should be more effective (entry 1). Disap-
pointingly, only the decomposition of 1ab to form a furfuryl aldehyde
was observed, which was attributed to the ready ring-opening of the
hemiacetal followed by recyclization (see Supplementary Table 1

binaphthol (BINOL)-derived CPA catalysts. Although the majority

Results and discussion
Reaction development
First, a family of pyranones 1 with the olefinic dipolarophiles tethered
at the 3-positions was prepared for reaction as the oxidopyrylium
precursors. In our initial attempts, we used acetoxypyranone 1aa as
substrate because this is a common precursor to oxidopyrylium ylides,
although they are typically generated under basic conditions<sup>30–33</sup>.
Unfortunately, in the presence of a chiral-phosphoric-acid (CPA)
catalyst, no reaction was observed (Table 1, entry 1). We also tried
the dual catalytic system with a chiral amine and an achiral thiourea,
developed for the type I cycloaddition by Jacobsen and co-workers<sup>26</sup>;
however, this system proved ineffective for the type II cycloaddition
(see Supplementary Table 1 for details). To improve the reactiv-
ity, hydroxypyranone 1ab was examined with the expectation that
acid-catalysed dehydration should be more effective (entry 1). Disap-
pointingly, only the decomposition of 1ab to form a furfuryl aldehyde
was observed, which was attributed to the ready ring-opening of the
hemiacetal followed by recyclization (see Supplementary Table 1
for details). To avoid this undesired ring-opening, we reasoned that
installing an alkoxy group should encourage productive elimination
towards oxidopyrylium formation. In the event, methoxypyranone
1ac was prepared and subjected to reaction to successfully gener-
ate the desired cycloadduct 2 in 40% yield, but with low enantiose-
lectivity using A1 as catalyst (entry 2). We then surveyed various
binaphthol (BINOL)-derived CPA catalysts. Although the majority
of these failed to substantially improve the enantioselectivity of the
cycloaddition, it was notable that the use of the very bulky CPA A3
bearing 2,6-dimethyl-4-t-butyl substituents at the 3,3′-positions
did dramatically increase the reaction e.e., albeit with a low yield
(64% e.e., 13% yield, entry 4). Next, we examined another series of
CPAs derived from 2,2′,3,3′-tetrahydro-1,1′-spirobi[phenalene]-
9,9′-diol (SPHENOL), a new rigid chiral backbone developed in our
own laboratory<sup>34</sup>. When B1 was used as catalyst, the reaction cleanly
afforded the desired cycloadduct 2 in 87% yield and 79% e.e. (entry 5).
Further optimizations of other reaction parameters (for example,
solvent, temperature, concentration) did not lead to obvious improve-
ments. However, we noted that the protective group on the nitrogen
atom in the linker influenced the enantioselectivity of the reaction.
Replacing the Ts with Ps (phenylsulfonyl) resulted in substrate 1a
undergoing cycloaddition with improved enantioselectivity (90% e.e.,
entry 8). In comparison, catalyst A3 showed very low catalytic activity
(6% yield, entry 9). Not surprisingly, the reaction was not sensitive
to the concentration (entry 10). Decreasing the temperature did not
greatly improve the enantioselectivity, but significantly compromised
the chemical yield (entry 11). Finally, the use of activated 4-Å molecular
sieves was essential to achieve a high yield of the enone product 2, by
capturing the methanol by-product that would otherwise readily add
to the highly reactive bridge-head double bond to form the conjugate
adduct 2′. In fact, without molecular sieves, 2 was isolated in only 17%
yield, whereas 2′ was obtained in 55% yield (entry 12).

Scope of 8-azabicyclo[4.3.1]decanes
Using this optimized protocol (Table 1, entry 9), a series of enanti-
omerically enriched 8-azabicyclo[4.3.1]decanes were successfully
generated under mild conditions, with good yields and excellent enan-
tioselectivities (Fig. 2). Pyranones bearing extended alkyl chains at the
2-position (1b, 1c) underwent reaction with similar yields and enan-
tioselectivities. Moreover, pyranones bearing alkoxymethyl groups
at C2 (1d, 1e), which allow further manipulations at those positions,
were smoothly converted into the desired products 2d and 2e with
good yields and excellent enantioselectivities (90% e.e.). Substrate
1f with allyl substitution at this position proved compatible as well,
resulting in 2f with a good enantioselectivity (88% e.e.) and a modest
yield. The pyranone bearing a 1,1-disubstituted olefin (1g) also reacted
smoothly to generate 2g having vicinal tetrasubstituted stereocentres
at bridge-head positions. It should be noted that the installation of a
quaternary stereogenic carbon centre at the bridge-head position of
a polycyclic structure is a formidable challenge in organic synthesis<sup>35</sup>.
Besides terminal olefins, internal alkenes were also suitable for cycload-
dition, although a slightly higher reaction temperature was needed.
For example, pyranones 1h tethered to a 1,2-disubstituted double bond
and 1i bearing an even sterically more hindered trisubstituted double
bond both reacted smoothly at

enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity in a single step. An allene
(1k) was also a good cycloaddition substrate, although the reaction
proceeded with a slightly compromised yield and enantioselectivity.
Finally, acetal substrate 1l (as opposed to the others which are ketals)
also underwent cycloaddition, but the direct cycloaddition product
2l is very unstable toward addition to relieve anti-Bredt destabiliza-
tion. Thus, 2l was isolated as its methanolic adduct 2l′ by purposely
excluding molecular sieves.

[4.3.1]dodecane cycloadducts prompted us to further explore the reac-
tion of substrates with alternative tethers. For substrates bearing an
all-carbon tether between the olefin and pyranone, slight modifications
of the reaction conditions were needed to achieve the best outcomes.
For these substrates, BINOL-based CPA A4 was found to be a superior
catalyst, promoting the reaction with high efficiency and enantiose-
lectivities (see Supplementary Table 6 for more details). Among the
malonate-derived substrates (3a, 3b, 3c), 3c bearing sterically hindered
isopropyl ester groups reacted with the highest enantioselectivity. The
structure of cycloadduct 4c was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray
crystallography (CDCC 2340807). Variations of the substituent at the
2-position (the ketal carbon) of the pyranone (3c, 3d) did not result in
significant differences on the reactivity or enantioselectivity. Alkene
substrates with various substitution patterns, including 1,2- (3e, 3f) and
1,1-disubstituted double bonds (3g), and those that are electron-rich
(3e, 3g) and electron-poor (3f), all engaged in [5 + 2] cycloaddition with
good-to-excellent yields and enantioselectivities.

Synthetic applications
We conducted studies to demonstrate the utility and poten-
tial applications of these enantioselective [5 + 2] cycloadditions
(Fig. 4). The cycloadditions to generate the enantiomerically enriched
oxygen-bridged polycyclic products 2e and 4c could be scaled up to
>1-mmol scales efficiently, and with virtually no loss in yields or enan-
tioselectivities.
We also examined the transformations of the enantioenriched
products generated from our process. The anti-Bredt compound
2e is highly reactive. Thus 1,2-reduction and 1,4-addition from the
convex face proceeded readily to generate 5 and 6, respectively, in
excellent yields and as single diastereomers. The Diels–Alder reac-
tion of 2e with cyclopentadiene provided polycyclic 7 with 2.5:1 dias-
tereomeric ratio (d.r.) and 88% e.e. (major). It is also worth noting
that a compound closely related to 2e with its 8-azabicyclo[4.3.1]

synthesis of the natural product daphgraciline<sup>33</sup>. The bicyclo[4.3.1]
decane 4c could be hydrogenated to afford saturated ketone 8. Treat-
ment of 4c under Corey–Chaykovsky reaction conditions provided
cyclopropanated 9, and the reaction with an excess of the sulfoxo-
nium reagent further induced epoxidation to furnish 10 as a single
diastereomer.

Conclusion
We have developed a catalytic enantioselective type II [5 + 2] cycload-
dition reaction of oxidopyrylium ylides, a formidable challenge
that necessitates overcoming the formation of strained, anti-Bredt
cycloadducts bearing bridge-head double bonds while exerting enan-
tiocontrol. The process also represents the first demonstration of
non-covalent activation by a chiral acid catalysis for the challeng-
ing asymmetric induction of cycloadditions of oxidopyryliums, in
contrast the previously required covalent activation. The choice
of a suitable leaving group to facilitate the in situ generation of the
key 3-oxidopyrylium intermediate under acidic conditions proved
crucial to the success of these reactions. Notably, CPAs derived from
the SPHENOL backbone developed in our own laboratories proved
uniquely effective at inducing enantioselectivity in some of these
cycloadditions. The protocol provides various functionalized and
bridged carbocycles, which can serve as advanced intermediates in
complex molecule synthesis, a few of which are already the core struc-
tures of some important natural products and drug molecules. Our
mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations indicate that the reac-
tion pathway involves enolization as the rate-determining step prior
to elimination of the alkoxide to form the key 3-oxidopyrylium ylide
intermediate, which is followed by the enantiodiscriminating
cycloaddition. The chiral acid catalyst plays a dual role, serving as (1)
a promoter for the rate-determining enolization and (2) a source of
asymmetric induction for the enantioselective C–C bond formation.
This protocol is expected to be applicable to other cycloadditions and
would find more applications in the rapid synthesis and diversification
of other useful complex molecules.
Methods
Enantioselective synthesis of 8-azabicyclo[4.3.1]decanes
An oven-dried 20-ml vial was charged with 1 (0.3 mmol), 4-Å molecular
sieve (160 mg, 480 mg mmol<sup>−1</sup>), dry toluene (0.05 M, 6 ml) and (R)-B1
(10 mol%). The vial was sealed and allowed to stir at room temperature
and the progress was monitored by thin-layer chromatography. Next, the
mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure. The crude product
was purified by silica-gel flash chromatography (n-hexane/ethyl acetate,
10:1 → 3:1). The e.e. was determined by chiral high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) after chromatographic purification on silica gel.

Conclusion
We have developed a catalytic enantioselective type II [5 + 2] cycload-
dition reaction of oxidopyrylium ylides, a formidable challenge
that necessitates overcoming the formation of strained, anti-Bredt
cycloadducts bearing bridge-head double bonds while exerting enan-
tiocontrol. The process also represents the first demonstration of
non-covalent activation by a chiral acid catalysis for the challeng-
ing asymmetric induction of cycloadditions of oxidopyryliums, in
contrast the previously required covalent activation. The choice
of a suitable leaving group to facilitate the in situ generation of the
key 3-oxidopyrylium intermediate under acidic conditions proved
crucial to the success of these reactions. Notably, CPAs derived from
the SPHENOL backbone developed in our own laboratories proved
uniquely effective at inducing enantioselectivity in some of these
cycloadditions. The protocol provides various functionalized and
bridged carbocycles, which can serve as advanced intermediates in
complex molecule synthesis, a few of which are already the core struc-
tures of some important natural products and drug molecules. Our
mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations indicate that the reac-
tion pathway involves enolization as the rate-determining step prior
to elimination of the alkoxide to form the key 3-oxidopyrylium ylide
intermediate, which is followed by the enantiodiscriminating
cycloaddition. The chiral acid catalyst plays a dual role, serving as (1)
a promoter for the rate-determining enolization and (2) a source of
asymmetric induction for the enantioselective C–C bond formation.
This protocol is expected to be applicable to other cycloadditions and
would find more applications in the rapid synthesis and diversification
of other useful complex molecules.
Methods
Enantioselective synthesis of 8-azabicyclo[4.3.1]decanes
An oven-dried 20-ml vial was charged with 1 (0.3 mmol), 4-Å molecular
sieve (160 mg, 480 mg mmol<sup>−1</sup>), dry toluene (0.05 M, 6 ml) and (R)-B1
(10 mol%). The vial was sealed and allowed to stir at room temperature
and the progress was monitored by thin-layer chromatography. Next, the
mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure. The crude product
was purified by silica-gel flash chromatography (n-hexane/ethyl acetate,
10:1 → 3:1). The e.e. was determined by chiral high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) after chromatographic purification on silica gel.
Enantioselective synthesis of cycloadducts with bicyclo[4.n.1]
alkane cores
An oven-dried 20-ml vial was charged with 3 (0.25 mmol), 4-Å molecu-
lar sieve (120 mg, 480 mg mmol<sup>−1</sup>, stored in a glovebox), dry toluene
(0.05 M, 5 ml) and (R)-A4 (10 mol%). The vial was sealed and allowed to
stir at room temperature and the progress was monitored by thin-layer
chromatography. Next, the mixture was concentrated under reduced
pressure. The crude product was purified by silica-gel flash chromatog-
raphy (n-hexane/ethyl acetate, 10:1 → 4:1). The e.e. was determined by
chiral HPLC after chromatographic purification on silica gel.
